# Asātamantajātaka (Ja 61)

**ID:** Ja 61
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Asātamantajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Unpleasant Spell
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja61
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Asātamantajātaka* (Ja 61), translated as *The Unpleasant Spell*, is a narrative located in the *Itthi-vagga* of the *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral; Appleton 2010]. According to its introductory framework (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha related the tale at Jetavana to admonish a monk unsettled by lust, illustrating the destructive and degraded nature of sensual obsession [SuttaCentral; Lewis and Tuladhar 2000]. 

In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), a youth travels to Takkasilā to study under a renowned teacher [Migot 1954]. The teacher's aged and blind mother falls desperately in love with the student and even plots to kill her own son to pursue her desires [GLOBAL RECOVERY 2010; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. Confronted with this terrifying manifestation of unbridled craving, the youth experiences profound revulsion toward worldly life and gains permission from his parents to go forth as an ascetic [Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. The story concludes with the Master declaring the dangers of passion and teaching the Four Noble Truths [Lewis and Tuladhar 2000]. In the narrative's identification of births, the teacher was the Bodhisatta, the pupil was Ānanda, and the father was Mahākassapa [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Migot 1954].

Scholars classify Ja 61 as the opening text of a cluster of five jātakas (Ja 61–65) in the *Itthi-vagga* that treat themes of misogyny and sensual peril [Appleton 2010; Evola 1995]. Maurice Winternitz observed that this thematic clustering raises doubts about whether the verses of Ja 61–65 were originally intended for five distinct narratives or were reshaped and anthologized by later compilers [Winternitz 1933].

SuttaCentral records a curated passage-level parallel to the *Kuṇālajātaka* (Ja 536), which similarly catalogues narratives on the dangers of sensual craving [SuttaCentral; GLOBAL RECOVERY 2010]. DharmaNexus identified no automated Pali-internal text reuse or cross-language matches meeting the threshold score of 10 [DharmaNexus].
